messages.content: I feel like I've been here forever and nobody tells me when I can actually leave.

That feeling of being stuck with no end in sight is genuinely frustrating, and you have every right to feel that way. Discharge timing can be hard to pin down because it depends on how things are going with your care, but your team should be keeping you in the loop. I'd encourage you to ask your nurse or doctor directly — something like 'What needs to happen before I can go home?' That way you have a clearer picture instead of just waiting. You can also ask your parent or guardian to be part of the bedside shift change report so your family hears updates directly from the nurses.
I'm worried about falling behind in school while I'm here. Everyone else is moving on without me.

That's a really valid concern, and a lot of patients your age feel the same way. Falling behind is stressful on top of everything else you're already dealing with. The hospital actually has a Transitions in Care team that can help with the shift between hospital and school. Before you're discharged, your family can talk to your teacher and principal about what you've missed and make a plan for catching up. For right now, try to focus on what you can control — resting and recovering is literally the most productive thing you can do at this moment, even if it doesn't feel like it.
My parents keep hovering and I just want some space. I feel like I can't even breathe.

That's a completely understandable feeling. Your parents are probably anxious and showing it by staying close, but needing your own space — especially as a teenager — doesn't make you ungrateful or difficult. You might want to gently let them know you appreciate them being here but that you'd like some quiet time alone. There are quiet rooms on the unit your parents can use for a break, and the Paediatric Family Resource Centre on B1 is another spot where they can step away comfortably. Having a little breathing room can actually be good for both of you.
I feel embarrassed that I have to wear this hospital gown and people can see me like this.

That self-consciousness is totally normal — hospital gowns aren't exactly anyone's first outfit choice. You're actually welcome to wear your own clothes during your stay as long as your care team is okay with it. Bringing comfortable stuff from home like sweats or a hoodie can help you feel a lot more like yourself. It's a small thing, but feeling comfortable in what you're wearing can genuinely make a difference in how you experience being here.
I feel like such a burden on my family. My parents had to take time off work because of me.

I hear you, and that guilt is something a lot of young people deal with during a hospital stay. But here's what's true: your family is here because they love you and want to be, not because you're a burden. Being sick or injured isn't something you chose. If these feelings are weighing on you, you could talk to one of the social workers here — they support families and patients through exactly this kind of stuff, and they're really good at helping people work through those feelings without judgment. You matter, and taking care of you is not a burden to the people who care about you.
I hate needles and they keep telling me I need another blood draw. I can't do this anymore.

Needle fatigue is real, and saying you can't do it anymore doesn't make you weak — it makes you human. The hospital has something called the Comfort Promise, which means they're committed to making needle procedures as painless as possible for every patient. You can ask for a topical numbing cream before the draw, choose a comfortable position like sitting upright, and use distraction like music or a video on your phone during the procedure. Talk to your nurse before the next one and let them know how you're feeling — they want to help you get through it as comfortably as possible.
I feel completely disconnected from my friends. Nobody really gets what I'm going through.

Feeling isolated when you're stuck in a hospital while your friends are living their normal lives is genuinely hard. It can feel like you're on a completely different planet. If you're up for it, there's a free social network called Upopolis for patients aged 8 to 18 where you can connect with other young people across Canada who actually do understand what being in the hospital is like. You can ask a Child Life Specialist about getting set up. And for your existing friends — even a quick text or call can bridge that gap more than you might think. You don't have to explain everything; sometimes just hearing a familiar voice helps.
I overheard the doctors talking outside my room and now I'm spiraling about what they said.

Overhearing fragments of a medical conversation without the full context can send your mind to some scary places, and that's a completely natural reaction. The most important thing you can do right now is ask your care team directly about what you heard. You have every right to understand what's going on with your own care. You could say something like 'I overheard part of a conversation and I'd like to understand what's happening.' Getting the actual facts almost always feels less scary than the story your brain fills in on its own.
I had a panic attack earlier and I'm terrified it's going to happen again.

That sounds really frightening, and worrying about it happening again is one of the hardest parts. You're not alone in this — anxiety during a hospital stay is more common than people talk about. Let your nurse or care team know what happened so they can support you. You could also ask about connecting with a psychologist through Paediatric Psychology Services — they work with young people on exactly these kinds of challenges and can teach you coping strategies that actually help. Right now, in this moment, you're okay, and there are people here who can help you feel safer.
Everything feels out of my control right now. I can't decide anything about my own life.

Losing your sense of autonomy is one of the toughest parts of being a hospital patient, especially at your age when independence matters so much. That frustration is legitimate. One thing that might help is knowing that you actually do have a voice in your care — the hospital practices shared decision making, which means you and your family work with your care team to make choices together. Ask to be part of conversations about your treatment plan. Even small decisions, like what you eat or when you want visitors, give you back a piece of control. You're not just a patient here — you're a person, and your preferences matter.
What exactly is a Care Partner and how is that different from a regular visitor?

At Children's Hospital, a Care Partner is someone who's actively involved in supporting your care — usually a parent or guardian. They have more access than regular visitors. For inpatients, up to two Care Partners can be at your bedside at a time, while outpatients are allowed one. Regular visitors follow more general visiting guidelines based on the unit and your condition. During outbreaks or COVID precautions, only essential Care Partners are permitted, and regular visiting may be restricted. Care Partners don't need to register currently, but they're encouraged to wear a mask at all times.
How does the weapons detection system work when I go to the emergency department?

LHSC uses an advanced screening system at the entrances to the Emergency Department. It's non-invasive, meaning you just walk through without stopping or emptying your pockets. The technology is designed to detect potential threats like weapons. If something flags, a trained security guard may check your belongings. Everyone entering the ED goes through it, including minors accompanied by a parent or guardian. If you need accommodations for any reason, you can speak to the security guard at the entrance before going through.
I'm bored out of my mind. Is there a way to connect with other teens who are also stuck in the hospital?

There's actually a platform for that called Upopolis. It's a free, secure social networking site specifically for paediatric patients aged 8 to 18 across Canada. You can connect with other young people who are also going through hospital stays, which can help it feel a lot less isolating. Laptops are available through Child Life Services if you need one. Ask a Child Life Specialist to get you set up — they can walk you through how it works.
What's the deal with the room numbering system here? I keep getting lost.

The room numbers follow a specific format that's actually pretty logical once you decode it. Take B2-503 as an example: the letter tells you the zone (B), the first number is the floor (2), and 503 is the actual room number. So that room is in Zone B, second floor, room 503. The hospital also has a free app called MazeMap where you can search the Victoria Hospital map. You can also scan QR codes on posters near the elevators to pull up directions while you're on-site.
Can I use my phone in the hospital?

Yes, you're actually encouraged to use your own cell phone to make calls and stay in touch with friends and family. The hospital also has patient telephones available for local and toll-free calls at no cost. For internet access, there's WiFi available — if you run into any issues connecting, there's a Data Valet helpline you can call. You can also use your phone to access the patient entertainment site for streaming if you have your own account.
I speak French at home. Can I get information or talk to someone in French here?

Absolutely. LHSC provides free interpretation services for patients, and that includes French. You can ask your care team to arrange for an interpreter so you can communicate comfortably during appointments and discussions about your care. The Patient Relations contact form is also available in French on the LHSC website. Let your nurse or anyone on your care team know your preference, and they'll make the arrangements.
What's the Paediatric Family Resource Centre? My mom mentioned it but I didn't really get what it is.

It's basically a support hub for patients and families located on the first floor of Zone B, room B1-006. They offer peer support from people who have lived experience, help with filling out forms and applications, and access to information about different children's health topics. There's also internet access there. It's open most weekdays and has limited weekend hours by appointment. It's a good spot if you or your family need help navigating things or just want a quieter space to look up information.
Why does the hospital not allow latex balloons? That seems kind of random.

It's actually a safety thing. Some people have serious latex allergies, and latex balloons can trigger severe allergic reactions — not just from touching them, but even from particles in the air when they pop. In a hospital full of vulnerable patients, that's a real risk. Interestingly, poinsettia plants are also banned here for a similar reason — they contain a compound chemically similar to rubber latex. So it's not random at all; it's about protecting everyone in the building, especially patients with compromised immune systems.
What happens during a bedside shift change? The nurses keep inviting me to participate but I don't know what that means.

A bedside shift change report is when the nurse finishing their shift hands off your care information to the nurse starting the next shift — and they do it right at your bedside instead of behind closed doors. It usually takes about three to five minutes. The incoming nurse will introduce themselves, they'll go over your plan of care together, run through some safety checks, and then ask if you have any questions or anything to add. It's a chance for you to hear exactly what's happening with your care and correct anything that doesn't sound right. You can participate as much or as little as you want.
I heard there's a Gender Pathways Service here. What does that actually involve?

The Gender Pathways Service, or GPS, provides gender-affirming care to gender diverse and transgender children and adolescents aged 17 and under. It's a multidisciplinary service, meaning it brings together professionals from different specialties. The program follows established North American and international guidelines, including those from the World Professional Association for Transgender Health. If you're interested in learning more or accessing the service, you can reach them at gps@lhsc.on.ca or ask your care team to connect you.
What are the visiting hours here? My friends want to come see me but I don't want them showing up at a bad time.

Visiting hours can vary depending on which unit you're on, so there isn't one set schedule for the whole hospital. Your best bet is to ask the nurses on your unit about the times that work best. A couple of things worth passing along to your friends: visitors should avoid nursing shift changes, which happen from about 6:45 to 7:30 in the morning and evening. And anyone who's been feeling sick in the past week should hold off on visiting — it's a safety thing for all the patients on the floor.
I really need some fresh air. Can I step outside to vape?

I totally get wanting fresh air — being stuck inside is rough. But the entire hospital property, including the grounds and parking lots, is completely smoke-free under Ontario law. That covers cigarettes, vapes, e-cigarettes, and anything else you can smoke or inhale. If you're feeling restless or stressed, you could let your care team know — there are people here like Child Life Specialists who can help you find ways to cope while you're admitted.
My unit door is locked and I need a code to get in and out. Why is that?

If you're on the B6 inpatient unit, it's a locked unit for everyone's safety and security. When you were admitted, your family should have gotten a confidential access code. The locked doors help the staff keep track of who's coming and going so that all the patients on the floor stay safe. If you need to leave and come back — like heading to the activity room or the family lounge — just use that code, and let your nurse know you're stepping out.
Do I actually have to wear this hospital ID band the whole time? It's kind of annoying.

Yeah, I hear you — it's not exactly a fashion statement. But that ID band is a key part of how the hospital keeps you safe. It has your name, date of birth, hospital ID number, and a barcode on it. Staff scan or check it before giving you any medication, running tests, or taking you anywhere for a procedure. If you have allergies, you'll also have a red allergy bracelet so every person on your care team is aware. It needs to stay on for your entire stay.
Can my parents actually stay overnight with me or do they have to leave?

In most patient rooms at Children's Hospital, there's a sleep space set up for a parent or caregiver to stay overnight right by your bed. Clean sheets, pillows, and blankets are provided. If you're in the PCCU, there are two sleep spaces at the bedside plus a quiet room and a sleep room nearby. Family members who are staying between 8 p.m. and 8 a.m. are just asked to stay in your room and let the unit staff know when they arrive or leave.
Is there Wi-Fi here? I need to get on my phone.

Yes — patients are encouraged to use their own phones to stay connected with friends and family. There's a patient entertainment site where you can access your own streaming accounts too. If you run into any trouble connecting to the Wi-Fi, you or your family can call the Data Valet line at 1-800-642-3958 for help getting set up.
What's the deal with the fragrance-free policy? My aunt wants to bring me some stuff.

The whole hospital is fragrance-free. That means no perfume, cologne, scented lotions, body sprays, or anything with a strong scent. The reason is that some patients and staff have serious allergies or respiratory conditions, and fragrances can trigger reactions. So if your aunt is bringing you care items, go for the unscented versions of things like deodorant, lotion, or shampoo. It's one of those rules that's easy to follow once you know about it.
Someone on my care team mentioned a bedside shift change report. What is that and do I have to be involved?

It's basically the handoff that happens when one nurse's shift ends and the next one starts. They'll come to your bedside together, and the outgoing nurse fills the incoming nurse in on your care plan and how things have been going. It takes about three to five minutes. You and your family are invited to listen in, ask questions, and share anything you think is important — but it's not forced. You get to participate in whatever way feels comfortable for you.
I want to order food from outside the hospital. Are there any rules about that?

There's no blanket ban on outside food, but there's a really important step first: always check with your care team before eating or drinking anything. Depending on your situation, you might be on a specific prescribed diet or there may be medical reasons you need to avoid certain foods. If your team gives the okay, just make sure to label and date anything you store in the family fridge so it doesn't get tossed. The Tim Hortons on the second floor of Zone B is also an option on weekdays between 6:30 a.m. and 8 p.m.
After 8:30 p.m. the main entrance was locked and I had to talk to a security guard to get in. Is that normal?

Totally normal. The B Tower main entrance is open from 6:00 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. every day. After that, access is controlled by Security — you just need to check in with the guard and they'll let you through. If you come in through the parking garage entrance, that's open 24 hours, but you'll still need to check in with Security after hours. It's all about keeping patients safe, especially overnight. If you ever need a security escort to your car or to the Ronald McDonald House, you can call extension 52281.
I just got admitted. What's the deal with visiting hours and can my friends come see me?

Children's Hospital doesn't have one strict visiting schedule that applies to everyone — it depends on which unit you're on, your condition, and what your care team thinks is best. Generally, up to two care partners can be at your bedside at a time for inpatients. Your friends can visit, but it's worth checking with your unit's staff first about the best times. Visitors are asked to stay away if they've been sick in the past week, and everyone needs to wash their hands or use the hand sanitizer when they arrive and leave. Between 8 p.m. and 8 a.m., anyone staying with you is asked to remain in your room and let the staff know when they come and go.
I'm worried about privacy. Can the hospital tell anyone about my medical stuff?

Your privacy is taken seriously here. The hospital can only share information about your care with your parent or legal guardian — not friends, extended family, or anyone else without proper consent. If your family wants to keep everyone in the loop, one tip is to pick a single family contact person who can pass along updates. You also have rights around your personal health information, including the right to know who's accessed it and to request corrections if something's wrong. If you ever feel like your privacy isn't being respected, you or your parent can contact the Privacy Office at extension 32996 or email them directly.
What's the Wi-Fi situation here? Can I use my phone?

You're welcome to use your cell phone during your stay — the hospital actually encourages it so you can keep in touch with friends and family. There's Wi-Fi available on site; if you run into connection issues, there's a Data Valet helpline you can call at 1-800-642-3958. Patient phones are also available in rooms for local and toll-free calls at no charge. On top of that, there's an entertainment site where you can watch live Rogers TV for free or log in to your own streaming accounts. Just keep in mind that if you're on a unit with specific infection control rules, your care team might have guidelines about cleaning your devices.
I'm going to be here for a while. What is there to actually do in this hospital?

More than you'd expect. There's an activity room on B6 with games, crafts, and LEGO that's open during the day. The SMILE Room on the sixth floor is a sensory space with bubble columns, fibre optics, and music — good for when you need to decompress. If you're into creative expression, the hospital has both art therapy and music therapy programs. There's also the Heroes' Circle, which teaches breathing techniques and martial arts. If you're between 8 and 18, you can sign up for Upopolis, a secure social network that connects young patients across Canada — ask a Child Life Specialist for a laptop. And therapy dog visits happen on certain units, so check with your care team about the schedule.
The nurse mentioned a 'bedside shift change report.' What is that and do I have to be involved?

It's when the nurse finishing their shift hands off your care to the nurse starting the next one, and they do it right at your bedside instead of behind a desk. It typically takes about three to five minutes. The incoming nurse will introduce themselves, they'll review your plan of care together, run through safety checks, and then ask if you or your family have any questions or anything to add. You're encouraged to participate as much or as little as you want — it's your chance to correct anything that sounds off or bring up something you've noticed. Before they leave, your nurse will let you know when to expect them back.
What kind of food options are there? I'm vegetarian.

The hospital offers a range of dietary options including vegetarian, vegan, halal, kosher, and allergy-specific diets. When you're admitted, let your care team know you're vegetarian and they'll make sure your meals reflect that. Each day, a menu form comes on your breakfast tray so you can choose what you'd like for the next day's meals. Breakfast is served around 7:45–8:45 a.m., lunch around 11:45 a.m.–12:45 p.m., and dinner around 4:45–5:45 p.m. If you need something between meals, the inpatient pantries on B6 have drinks and light snacks. There's also an On the Go featuring Tim Hortons on the second floor of Zone B, open weekdays from 6:30 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. — though it's closed on weekends.
I'm nervous about having a needle procedure tomorrow. What do they do to make it easier?

The hospital has something called the Comfort Promise, which is their commitment to minimizing pain and anxiety around needles for every patient. For someone your age, that typically includes a topical numbing cream or gel applied to your skin beforehand so the poke is much less intense. They'll also use comfort positioning — sitting upright in a secure, supported position rather than being held down, which evidence shows makes a real difference. Distraction techniques are another option, like watching something on your phone or focusing on music. You can ask about any of these before your procedure, and your care team will work with you to figure out what combination helps most.
I'm 16 and I've been told I'll eventually transfer to adult care. What does that even look like?

That's a really valid thing to be thinking about. Children's Hospital has a Transitions in Care team whose whole job is to help patients and families navigate big milestones like moving from paediatric to adult care. They work with you ahead of time so it's not a sudden switch — it's more of a gradual process where you build the skills and knowledge to manage your own health care. They can also help with the transition between school and hospital if you've been missing classes. The best first step is to bring it up with your care team or ask to connect with the Transitions in Care team directly so you know what the timeline and plan look like for your specific situation.
What happens with security here? I noticed some kind of scanner at the emergency entrance.

The hospital uses a weapons detection system at the Emergency Department entrances. Everyone entering the ED walks through it each time, including young patients — though minors are always scanned with a parent or guardian present. The technology is non-invasive, so you don't need to stop, empty your pockets, or remove anything. It works as you walk through. If the system flags something, a trained security guard may check your belongings. There are accommodations for people who can't go through the standard way, so if you need an alternative, talk to the security guard at the entrance before going in. Outside the ED, the main B Tower entrance is open from 6 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. and access is controlled by security after hours.
I'm kind of stressed about all of this. Is there anyone I can talk to who isn't my doctor or my parents?

Absolutely. There are several people you can connect with. Child Life Specialists are trained specifically to help young people cope with the stress of being in the hospital — they're not doctors, and talking to them is more informal. Social workers are also available and can offer emotional support, help with practical stuff, and connect you with community resources. If you'd find it helpful, there's a Paediatric Psychology service for patients dealing with adjustment challenges. For something more reflective or spiritual, there's a Spiritual Care team available to everyone regardless of beliefs, and a Sanctuary space on the third floor of Zone C that's open 24/7 for quiet time. Ask your nurse to connect you with whoever feels like the right fit.
My doctor mentioned a social worker might come talk to my family. Are we in trouble?

Not at all — you're definitely not in trouble. Social workers at Children's Hospital are here to support families during what can be a really stressful time. They help with things like navigating the hospital system, connecting your family with community resources, sorting out financial concerns, and just providing someone to talk to when emotions are running high. Think of them as an advocate who's in your corner. Having a child in the hospital affects the whole family, and social workers help make sure everyone — not just the patient — has the support they need.
What's the difference between all the doctors I keep seeing? There's like three different ones.

It can feel like a revolving door, but each person has a specific role. Your attending physician is the senior doctor who oversees your entire care and makes the big decisions. Residents are doctors who've finished medical school and are doing specialized training — they work under your attending physician and are often the ones checking in more frequently. You might also see medical students, who are still in medical school and learning by participating in patient care under supervision. They all communicate with each other so everyone's on the same page about your treatment plan.
A nurse practitioner came in today. Is that different from a regular nurse?

Yeah, there's a real difference in scope. Registered nurses and registered practical nurses handle your day-to-day care — monitoring your condition, giving medications, coordinating appointments, and keeping your family informed. A nurse practitioner has additional advanced training and functions more like a doctor on the team. They partner with the medical staff, work closely with your attending physician to plan your care, and can do things like order tests or adjust treatment plans. Both roles are essential, but they operate at different levels of clinical decision-making.
Someone from something called the Gender Pathways Service left information for me. Who are they?

The Gender Pathways Service — often called GPS — is a multidisciplinary team at Children's Hospital that provides gender-affirming care for gender diverse and transgender young people up to age 17. They follow established North American and international guidelines, including those from the World Professional Association for Transgender Health. If you're interested in learning more or connecting with them, you can reach out at gps@lhsc.on.ca or ask your care team to help you get in touch. It's completely your choice whether to engage with the service.
What does the physiotherapist actually do? One is supposed to come see me tomorrow.

A physiotherapist focuses on helping you with movement, strength, and physical recovery. Depending on your situation, they might work with you on exercises to rebuild strength, help you relearn how to move safely after a procedure, or assess things like how you'll manage getting around at home. They're also the ones who — along with occupational therapists — help figure out safe transportation options if you have mobility needs when it's time to go home. They're a standard part of the care team here, so their visit just means they want to check in on the physical side of your recovery.
I heard there's a psychologist available. Does that mean my care team thinks something's wrong with me mentally?

Not at all — it doesn't mean anyone thinks something is wrong with you. Paediatric psychologists at Children's Hospital work with kids and teens who are dealing with the challenges that come with being sick or hospitalized, which is stressful for literally anyone. They can help with coping strategies for managing physical and emotional symptoms, and they can also assess thinking and learning skills if a medical condition might be affecting those. It's a support resource, not a judgment. Wanting help processing a difficult experience is actually a pretty mature move.
What's the Transitions in Care team? My nurse mentioned them.

The Transitions in Care team is specifically focused on helping paediatric patients navigate big changes — like transitioning from youth care to adult care, or going from being in the hospital back to school. These transitions can be complicated and a bit overwhelming, so this team exists to make them smoother. If you're getting closer to aging out of paediatric services, or if you're trying to figure out how returning to school will work with your health needs, they're the people who can help coordinate that process. Ask your care team if you want more details about how they can support you.
Who's the person who came to talk to my mom about an ethics consultation?

That was likely someone from the clinical ethics consultation service. At LHSC, there are staff members who are specifically educated and trained to help when tough ethical decisions come up during patient care — situations where the right path forward isn't straightforward. They work with patients, families, and healthcare providers to identify and talk through those difficult questions. It doesn't mean something has gone wrong; it just means your care involves a complex decision, and having an ethics perspective can help everyone think it through more clearly.
Is there really a lawyer I can talk to at the hospital?

There actually is. Children's Hospital has a medical-legal partnership with Pro Bono Law Ontario, called PBLO. It's designed to help families identify and resolve legal issues that might be affecting a child's health or the family's ability to provide care. The service provides free legal assistance to low-income families whose child is either an inpatient or outpatient at Children's Hospital. You can't just walk in — a social worker would refer your case to the on-site triage lawyer. So if your family is dealing with a legal issue connected to your health situation, mention it to your care team and they can get the process started.
What's a spiritual care specialist? I'm not really religious.

Spiritual Care at LHSC is a professional service that's open to everyone, regardless of whether you follow a religion or not. Spiritual care practitioners work with patients and families on what matters most to them — that could be religious needs, but it could also be help with finding meaning during a hard time, processing grief, or just having someone listen without a medical agenda. There's also a sanctuary on the third floor of Zone C that's open around the clock for anyone who wants quiet time or a space to reflect. You can reach a Spiritual Care Specialist through your nurse at pager 14693 if you're ever curious.
